10040-aleutian-indian-and-english-dictio:
Charles A. Lee compiled this Alaska Indian dictionary in 1896, giving common words in the dialects of the Aleutian Indian language. It covers the speech of the Oogashik, Egashik, Egegik, Anangashuk, and Misremie tribes around the Sulima River and neighboring parts.

The book pairs Aleutian words with English, offering a practical word list for traders, missionaries, and travelers in Alaska. Its value today is documentary: a record of languages and dialects as spoken in the nineteenth century. Linguists and historians of Alaska will find it a rare, useful survival for study today.
10341-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Charles F. Horne edited this twenty-first volume of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a series that retells world history in the words of leading scholars. Each volume arranges events in date order, with short introductions, notes, and reading lists to link the pieces. The plan claims no party, sect, or section bias.

This volume covers recent events around 1910 and 1911, from a house of governors in the United States to the union of South Africa and Portugal's turn to a republic. Finland under pressure, fast miles, and the fall of Diaz in Mexico also appear. Readers get a readable, early twentieth-century survey of a world on the move.
20801-some-remains-hitherto-unpublished-:
A changed word, from advice to direction, shows how Joseph Butler polished his thought. Some Remains gathers papers Butler never published in his life. Notes at the close of fragments show fresh ink where he reworked a line.

Butler, Bishop of Durham, wrote the famed Analogy of Religion in the 1700s. His sermons on human nature still shape moral thought today. These scraps let readers watch a careful mind at work in private. Scholars prize such remains for the light they throw on how a great thinker's views took their final shape.
2363-incognita-or-love-and-duty-reconcil:
William Congreve's early novel Incognita, or Love and Duty Reconcil'd, is a Restoration comedy in prose, full of disguises, mistaken lovers, and witty intrigue. Written when Congreve was still young, it follows Aurelian and Hippolito through a maze of love affairs in Florence, where duty and desire keep crossing. The prose sparkles with the wit that would fill his plays.

The novella is short, fast, and deliberately artificial, a game of masks and revelations. It shows Congreve learning the comic timing of The Way of the World. Readers of Restoration literature will enjoy this rare prose piece.
3617-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Alexandre Dumas's Celebrated Crimes, the ninth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Dumas, famous for The Three Musketeers, also wrote a series of true crime histories about murder, poison, and intrigue in European courts. This file lifts short passages from those crime stories for browsing.

Readers meet Dumas's dramatic voice in brief form: tales of poisoners, queens, and assassins told with novelist's flair. The set works as a sampler for those curious about his nonfiction and as a source of short lines. His full Celebrated Crimes give the trials, escapes, and executions that these extracts only hint at.
6721-the-voyages-of-captain-scott-retold:
Charles Turley retells Captain Robert Scott's voyages from The Voyage of the Discovery and Scott's Last Expedition, with an introduction by J. M. Barrie. Pictures in color and black and white, plus a map, aid the tale. The Discovery chapters run from southward ho to winter quarters, a polar winter, and a southern journey, then a second winter and release.

The last expedition chapters follow stormy seas, depôt laying at One Ton Camp, and perils that end in tragedy. Turley writes for young readers, with a hero's tale told plainly. The Voyages of Captain Scott is a moving, classic retelling of Antarctic courage and loss.
6989-ancient-rome-from-the-earliest-time:
Robert Pennell wrote Ancient Rome as a companion to his History of Greece, for high schools and academies wanting a short clear account of Rome's rise and fall. The revised edition was wholly rewritten, with new matter added to meet recent requirements and the penults of proper names marked long in text and index. Lives of chief men join an outline of institutions, manners, and religion.

Examination papers show the present range of requirement in leading colleges, and maps and plans were specially drawn and engraved for the book. Names and places not in the text were mostly left off the maps, to keep them clear and open. Pennell aims at a school history that is brief, orderly, and easy to use.
7808-grand-daddy-whiskers-m-d:
Nellie M. Leonard's Grand-Daddy Whiskers, M.D., pictured by Carle Michel Boog, sends a woodland doctor to work among animal folk. A message from the woodfolk leads back to the lake, where Grand-Daddy begins his rounds, Dot Squeaky holds summer school, and a woods fire tests them all.

Later chapters bring a busy day, twin tails, Wiggle borrowing an automobile, autumn leaves, and being snowed in. Pictures show blindfold games, a call to Pond Lily Lake, a broken limb set deftly, and a band playing Silvy's Waltz. It is a cozy animal tale of care, courage, and neighbors helping.
9803-memoirs-of-the-life-and-corresponde:
Volume two of John Knox Laughton's Memoirs of Henry Reeve covers Reeve's later life, from the Italian war to retirement. Chapters follow the war in Italy, literature and politics, law and letters, and church politics. The Franco-German war, the Greville memoirs, and Foxholes follow, with French royalists and a final change. Reeve, editor and man of letters, moves through Europe's great hours.

Laughton draws on Reeve's letters and diaries, with a portrait from a Rupert Potter photograph. The volume opens with Orsini's 1858 attempt on Napoleon III. A reader gets a rich Victorian life, told through letters, wars, and literary London.
9822-mrs-mary-robinson-written-by-hersel:
Mary Robinson, the actress and poet known as Perdita, wrote her own life story, and this edition adds lives of the Duchesses of Gordon and Devonshire. Robinson rose from a difficult youth to the London stage, where her beauty and talent made her one of the most talked-about women of her day.

Her memoir moves through theatre, fashion, love affairs, and debt with unusual frankness for its time. The added duchess biographies set her beside two other famous society women. Together they paint Georgian high society from inside, in the voices of women who lived at its center.
ancient-rome-from-the-earliest-times-dow:
Robert F. Pennell designed his history, by his preface, as a companion to his History of Greece. It fills a want in high schools and academies. They needed a short, clear statement of the rise and fall of Rome. It adds biography of her chief men. It outlines her institutions, manners, and religion. This revised edition was entirely rewritten, with maps and plans drawn for the book.

Fifty chapters run from the geography of Italy and the Tarquin dynasty to the plebeians' contest for rights and the Punic Wars. Caesar and Cicero, the empire, and the long decline to the year 476 follow. Examination papers at the back show the college standard of the day. Pennell's compact survey served classrooms for decades.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDallasInvent: An FBI teletype sent on November 24, 1976 to the House Select Committee on Assassinations concerned inventories of records held in Dallas. The committee was then reopening the investigation of President Kennedy's death, and it needed to know what records existed. The surviving record gives the teletype's sender, recipient, date, and subject, but not the inventory itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FortDetrickBiol: Richard Lebherz wrote a piece titled Deterrent No. 7 about the biological warfare program at Fort Detrick, the Army's center for that work in Maryland. Germ warfare was a secret program discussed in public only in fragments. The surviving record gives the author, the title, and the subject but no date or contents, so the piece stands as a named article on the Detrick program.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GlanzeWalterD_G: A letter filed under the name Walter D. Glanze explains the writer's attempt to secure a 60,000 dollar unsecured loan. The money was meant to pay off a debt to the Internal Revenue Service. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled text, so the letter survives as an unsigned account of one man's effort to borrow his way clear of the tax service.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JonesRonaldCoyD:
The Dallas County Medical Society issued a program for an evening at The Science Place on October 27, 1999. The guest was Dr. Ronald C. Jones. Jones had been Parkland Hospital's chief resident on November 22, 1963, and he relived his experience of the day President Kennedy was shot.

Doctors who worked on the dying president carried the day with them for life. Thirty-six years later, a hometown medical audience heard the chief resident tell it again. The program preserves the billing of that evening, when Dallas medicine remembered its most famous emergency in public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinJohnJrDal:
FBI agents interviewed John Martin, Jr. on April 2, 1964, about a film he had made. Martin was superintendent of safety at the Dallas Post Office Terminal Annex. On November 22, 1963, he filmed the presidential motorcade with an 8mm movie camera. He then gave the film to Life magazine.

Amateur films of the motorcade became some of the most studied evidence in the case. Each one fixed the cars, the crowd, and the timing from a different spot. Martin's interview records who he was, where he stood, and what happened to his film afterward. It is the bureau's account of a witness whose evidence was pictures rather than words.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PatchenJerryD_P:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Jerry Patchen on December 15, 1974. He discusses the murder of Harvey St. Jean, a Miami lawyer. He also reports on his own affairs: the sales of his book, and his appearances on radio. Patchen was one of the correspondents with whom Weisberg shared case news.

The letter mixes the two registers of Weisberg's mail. First, a violent death in Miami that touched his network. Second, the business of being a self-published author: copies sold, broadcasts done. Letters like this kept his circle informed between book releases. They also show how much of his operation ran on personal correspondence, typed one letter at a time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PepperWilliamFD:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum on September 25, 1995, about a book by William Pepper. Pepper, a lawyer, had written on the King assassination. Weisberg says he distrusted Pepper for seeking access to his files without disclosing the book project. The memo also sets out Weisberg's criticism of the book itself.

Weisberg's files were his life's work, and he guarded them fiercely. A younger researcher asking for help while hiding a book struck him as a breach. The memo is written in his blunt late style, part grievance and part review. It records a falling-out between two men who agreed on much about the King case, and it shows how the movement's alliances broke on questions of credit.
govdocs-archive_org-tubes-4_Subterrene_N: A compilation called tubes-4 gathers material on subterrene machines, nuclear tunneling, and deep underground military bases. Its own file name adds the Illuminati and Freemasons to the mix. The library holds the set as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. It serves readers who study underground-base lore, a durable branch of conspiracy writing about hidden places beneath the American desert.
holbach-letters-to-eugenia-microform-on-: Letters to Eugenia, microform, on the absurd, contradictory, and demoralizing, by Holbach. The atheist's letters. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-d:
Part D is the fourth of six parts in the 1860 Virtue edition of David Hume's History of England. Hume wrote the history from 1754 to 1762, after his philosophy had met with cool reviews. The public took the history to its heart instead, and it stayed the standard account of England for generations.

From Caesar to 1688, Hume traces the slow growth of English law, liberty, and crown power. He writes as a judge above the fray, or tries to, and readers of every party quoted him. The edition holds the full seventy-one chapters across its six parts. Part D carries the story through its later, richer centuries.
incognita-or-love-and-duty-reconcil-d:
William Congreve wrote Incognita, a short prose romance of love and duty reconciled, before his fame as a dramatist of the Restoration stage. Congreve sets the tale in Florence, where two friends, Aurelian and Claudio, fall for ladies met at a tournament and a ball. Incognita is the name one heroine hides behind, and mistaken identity, disguise, and a near-duel keep the pairs apart.

Fathers, an unexpected marriage contract, and the claims of duty tangle the courtships before the reconciling of the title sorts them. Congreve tells it in balanced, witty prose that already shows the playwright's ear. The novella is brief enough for one sitting and polished enough to reward it, an early work by the author of The Way of the World.
memoirs-of-the-life-and-correspondence-o:
John Knox Laughton wrote the life and correspondence of Henry Reeve. Volume two of the two volume set stands here. Laughton taught modern history at King's College, London.

A portrait shows Reeve at sixty eight, from a photograph. Chapter thirteen treats the war in Italy, 1859 to 1860. Later heads treat law, letters, and church politics through the years. The Greville Memoirs, the Franco-German War, and his last years close the list. Outrage and disloyalty, French royalists, and retirement end the heads. A full life in law and letters fills the second volume.
mrs-mary-robinson-written-by-herself-wit:
Mary Robinson wrote these memoirs of her own life, paired here with lives of two duchesses. The editor calls her one of the most famed beauties of her day. Her dark eyes and sad air drew lords and princes. The Prince of Wales was among her admirers.

Garrick, Sheridan, Fox, and Reynolds were her friends. The book shows her at the Pantheon amid lamps and music. It gives bright scenes of fashionable life in her time. Grace and Philip Wharton shaped this deluxe edition. Robinson's own brief sketch stays vivid, a star's view of the world that adored and judged her.
nasa-tm-19630007589-investigation-of-the:
Donald D. Arabian of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-268. It studies roll behavior in two hypersonic gliders. Both gliders had curved, parabolic wing outlines. Tests ran at high subsonic speeds, just below sound.

Arabian measured rolling stability derivatives for each glider. In plain words, those numbers say how strongly a craft resists roll. They also say how roll damps out or grows worse. A glider slowing from orbit must not spiral out of control. Data at high subsonic speed covered the last stage before landing. The study helped judge whether these sleek shapes could be flown home safely.
nasa-tm-19630010655-free-flight-measurem:
Simon C. Sommer, Barbara J. Short, and Dale L. Compton of Ames wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-373, in August 1960. It reports free-flight tests of Mercury capsule models. The models flew at Mach 3 and at Mach 9.5. Mercury was America's first manned space program.

The team measured how steady the capsule shape flew in free flight. Both still stability and moving, dynamic stability were checked. A blunt capsule must fall heat shield first, without tumbling. Bad tumbling could kill a crew on the way down. These model flights, shot to high speed, proved the capsule's shape would hold its path in real reentry.
nasa-tm-19650025610-a-study-of-launch-ve:
Harold C Lester and Harold B Tolefson at Langley examined how a launch vehicle answers the fine detail of the wind, not just its average strength. Wind changes with height in small, sharp steps. A climbing rocket meets those steps in seconds. The pair presented their study at a meteorology meeting in Atlantic City in March 1964.

Their paper asks whether the small variations matter, or only the broad profile. If detail matters, launch rules based on smooth profiles could mislead. The work links weather measurement to vehicle loads in a direct way. Range staff and designers both needed that answer before committing a vehicle to flight.

two-dyaloges-c-1549-wrytten-in-laten-by-:
Two dialogues by Erasmus of Rotterdam, printed at Canterbury by John Mychell about 1549, appear in Edmonde Becke's English translation. One dialogue is called Polyphemus, or the Gospeller. The other treats of things and names. The old spelling of the title page is kept throughout.

Becke's preface to the reader quotes Seneca on requests from superiors that carry the force of commands. A near cousin, nearer still in friendship, pressed him to translate the dialogues. Becke owed the man service and himself besides, and dreaded the fault of ingratitude. Tudor readers thus received Erasmus's Latin wit dressed in the English of Henry's reign.
